newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine business tells Cavallo put up or shut up.
newsitem.headline: Argentine business tells Cavallo put up or shut up.

text.p: Tired of political upheaval, Argentina's business community is urging former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo to prove his corruption charges in court or stop making unsettling allegations.

"We cannot go on talking forever. Otherwise, anybody will talk, but will not prove what he says," Diego Videla, a top executive with the powerful Argentine Industrial Union lobby told Reuters. "People want things clarified, but oppose anyone just using the mass media and then seeing nothing happen."
After two weeks of front page coverage of a crossfire between Cavallo and members of cabinet, Videla's mood appears to be shared by other business leaders.
"Cavallo's accusations make lots of noise and stop investment projects, hold back long-term growth and raise country-risk," said an economist at a leading consultancy.
"I feel that this situation has only one solution and that is to go to court. Otherwise, Cavallo will lose credibility," said the economist, who asked for anonymity.

President Carlos Menem's former "superminister", who led Argentina out of decades of inflation into economic stability but was fired three months ago, accused two cabinet members of manipulating judges and covering up graft investigations.

Cavallo also said Menem's chief of staff, Alberto Kohan had indicated he was aware that government officials had paid bribes to secure a contract between state-run Banco Nacion and the U.S. computer giant IBM's local branch.
Cavallo said Kohan made those remarks at a meeting the two held with Menem. Both Menem and Kohan deny such meetings ever took place.
Even the current economy minister's cabinet chief, Carlos Rodriguez, a man close to Cavallo's orthodox economic philosphy, told the former minister to stop talking for the good of the country.
"His political cannibalism only helps raise the country-risk," he said.

But analysts, who have been tracking Cavallo's moves for years, say there is nothing to be surprised at. Even while he was in government, Cavallo was known for throwing tantrums in cabinet meetings, clashing with colleagues and threatening Menem to quit if he did not get his way.
"Every time he felt under pressure, he responded the same way," said leading political scientist Natalio Botana. "His style is extremely combative."
Nonetheless, analysts suggest it could be time for Cavallo to change that style. Economist Manuel Solanet said Cavallo should drop "the strategy of attacking as the best way to defend himself.
"Other ministers went through the same things he did. They put up with it, and years later they got the judicial rulings they sought," he said.

And Cavallo might just be ready to listen. In an interview to the La Nacion daily published Tuesday, he said: "Many friends have suggested my public statements create some distress. I want to prevent that from occuring so I have decided to stop talking."

But some felt Cavallo's airing of dirty laundry was to the good. "I believe businessmen do not want anyone to make waves. They do not seem to mind about the truth to (Cavallo's) the allegations," said political analyst James Neilson, who is based in Pinamar, Argentina. "That's absurd".
